title: Faith and mind, not two
hookLine: the poem ends: faith and mind are not two
carry: not two, and not clinging to one

lines: SOME POEMS END ON AN IMAGE.
cards: Some poems save their biggest image for the last line: a sunset, a storm, a door closing. The Xinxin Ming does something stranger.
It ends by taking its own title, faith and mind, and folding the two words together until there is no gap between them.
After all the warnings, about picking and choosing, the hair's breadth, the opinions, the last word it leaves is a pair of plain words. Not two.

teach.b: In paraphrase, the poem closes: faith and mind are not two; not two is faith in mind. Then it says the way is beyond words, not a matter of past, future or present. Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say faith and mind are one.
Because one is just another thing to hold. Earlier the poem has a line for exactly this: two exists because of one, so don't cling even to the one.

Chinese Buddhist texts use this word, not two, for what English often calls nonduality, and its whole job is to stop the mind landing anywhere: not split into two, and not stuck on one either. It's also practical.
In paraphrase, the poem advises: if you want to come into accord with the way quickly, just say: not two. Some translators add, when doubt arises.
It's less a doctrine to agree with than a tool to use, right when the mind starts dividing the moment into what I want and what I don't.
And the title folds shut. The poem began with picking and choosing, the mind splitting its day into liked and disliked.
It ends with the trust and the mind that trusts refusing to come apart. No faith standing over here, aimed at a mind over there. In the poem's last breath, the trusting and the trusted are not two.
Back where the week started: the great way is not hard.

how: Zen and Chan students who chant the Xinxin Ming end on these lines, and some teachers offer 'not two' as a phrase to return to in sitting when the mind starts to divide.

o: a pair of opposites always at war
neither split in two nor stuck on one

p: not two, says the poem's end
to accord with the way quickly

s: the poem ends by saying everything is one
it says not two, and warns elsewhere not to cling even to the one.
the poem gives 'not two' as something to say, not only a doctrine
to come into accord quickly, it says, just say: not two.
the last lines fold the poem's title together
faith and mind are not two; not two is faith in mind.

games.q: you've just heard 'not two' and decided: so everything is one. the poem has a line for this. what does it say?
o: good: now hold on to the one
two depends on one, so don't cling even to the one
one and two are both wrong, so stop sitting
games.why: the poem won't let the mind land on 'one' either. not two is meant to keep it from settling anywhere.

practice: Let the hands rest in the oval from earlier in the week, thumb tips just touching, and feel the point where they meet: which thumb is touching, and which is being touched?

Gently look for the line where one stops and the other starts, without forcing it or deciding anything. If a thought comes, like is this right, answer it the way the poem does, quietly, not two, and come back to the thumbs.

wordCard.voice: Not two. The last word of the Xinxin Ming: faith and mind are not two, and the poem won't let you settle on one either. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (bu er): 'not two', the poem's last word and a term Chinese Buddhist texts use for nonduality.

carryVoice: Your line: not two, and not clinging to one. Not split in two, and not stuck on one. The poem is finished; see you tomorrow.
